links.reason: Naladiyar 51 says sin cannot stand before austerity (தவத்தின்முன் நில்லாதாம் பாவம்) and returns when merit is spent; 343 only likens the going of darkness at sunrise to evil deeds leaving when old good deeds come forward (தொல்லை நல்வினை முற்படத் தோன்றிய அல்லல் வெவ்வினை போல அகன்றதே). That is a stock simile, and nothing in 343 points to her tapas, so the 'forecast' and 'doctrinal warrant' are read in.

2052 says heaven holds only plays, Indra's company and jewelled terraces (பிறிதில்லை); Naladiyar 137 is a conditional refusal to visit heaven if learned company is sweeter. Both belittle heaven, so this is agreement, not a qualification, and the teaches line leans on 2067 which is outside the packet, and no 'human measure' appears in 2052.

514 is Sitattan's self-reproach (பொருளைப் பொருளென்று கொண்டாய்), not a reproach by others, and 533 is narrator description of a city's streets, with nobody named as entering it. Two verses with different claims are not a tension, and the 'answer' to the wreck is a reconstructed plot, not something the Tamil states.

1965 lists beasts killed for deities that take offerings (பலிபெறு தெய்வங்கள் மேலிட்டுப் பாற்றும்) among their torments; Kural 259 ranks not killing above a thousand sacrifices. Both reject sacrifice, so the type is agrees rather than qualifies, but the victim's-side cost the epic adds is real though small.

1169 says great kings are laughed at for raging against a lowly foe (நகைசெயப் படுவதன்றே); it does not say the lowly cannot defeat the great. Kural 500 is about mud that sinks the elephant's feet (காலாழ் களரில்). The claims are not incompatible, so 'tension' is a shared jackal image dressed up.

1181 asks whether the war is of men, of gods or of both; 1200 has the prince say the matter rests with him (என்னொடு படுவதன்றே) and names no kind of war. It is story sequence in one council scene, not an answer to the question, and both units carry uncertain-sense flags.
links.text_issue: speakers in 1181 and 1200 are inferred from neighbouring verses

links.reason: 9 says the king, dense with desire, would not hear counsel (சொல்லாறு கேளான்), which fits Kural 448 on the king with no rebukers. But the Kural says nothing about having them, so the epic illustrates the couplet more than it limits it.

260 is the councillor's resigned list of what will kill the king (தான் செய்த பிழைப்புக் கொல்லும்), spoken to Kattiyangaran; 269 is the king consoling Vijayai with deed-fruit (தம் வினைப் பயத்தின் ஆகும்). They are different scenes, and the king is not answering any blame, so 'softens a blame' is read in. The contrast of causes is real but a tension, not a qualification.

241 has Kattiyangaran put his murderous wish on a possessing deity (மாதெய்வம்); 250 answers that the deity of his own words is no worthy guide (மாண்டது அன்று நின் வாய்மொழித் தெய்வமே). That claim-and-answer is real, but the teaches line relies on 247 making the king the deity, which 250 does not say.

2094 has the princes ask what fault they did (யாம் அடிகளைப் பிழைத்தது என்) and 2106 has them call their quarrelsome prattle foolish (பிணங்கிநாம் பிதற்றிய பேதை வாய்மொழி). Between them is a quarrel the pair does not show, so 'first grief turning to acceptance' is an inference from sequence.

Kural 545 ties rain and harvest to the just sceptre; 2583 shows fish leaping, deer fattening and killing banished under one rule (கொலைகடிந்து இவறல் இன்றிக் கோத்தொழில் நடத்தும்) with no rain at all. It is an extension to a golden age, but the claim that this shows the couplet's limit is not in either text.

Ainkurunuru 116 line 4 (காலை அன்ன காலை முந்துறுத்து) is uncertain and the 'morning swallowed too' reading rests on it. Kural 1225 asks what harm she did evening and what good to morning, and the claim that the couplet 'tidies' an older poem is a chronology the Tamil does not give.

44 compares death and birth to loosing a cloth and leaving a house (ஆடை, மாடம்), Kural 339 to sleep and waking. Both are consoling similes for death, but the claim that one is 'in the soul's hands' and the other not is not in either; the cloth and house are also not obviously a choice.

66 shows Yugi recovering and rising (தேறினன் எழுந்திருந்து) after the blow, which limits Kural 597's picture of strong minds who do not give way. That limit is real, but the fall itself is in 65 outside the unit, and no word is shared, so it is an illustration.

684 is a woman's joy at being adorned and touched (கையினாற் றீண்டப் பெற்றேன்); 2598 is a field-figure for the lute-lord enjoying the harvest of love. The 'promise and what became of it' and the ripened-field image are not in 684, and the woman of 2598 is only the marker's reading.

944 gives similes for the host's elephants, banners and warriors (கருவரை வருவன எனவுள களிறுகள்); Kural 768 says an army's martial bearing wins standing even without strength (படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்). 944 does not speak of standing at all, so it is a shared topic of an army's look, not a qualification.

520 is Dharan's promise to give back the companions 'without any deceit' (வஞ்சமொன்றின்றி), which the story keeps; no falsehood is told in the verse. The staged wreck and the king's purpose come from other verses, so the claim that this tests Kural 292 rests on a reconstructed plot.

162 has the king searching for the father's lost treasure; 163 has a speaker show him a great treasure and the two live in goodwill (மாநிதி காட்டி). That is a real answer of search by finding, but the speaker is unnamed and the 'trust that follows' is partly guessed.
links.text_issue: speaker of 163 unnamed; line 4 (பானலங் கிளவி) hard

links.reason: 2233 has the Earth, unable to bear the sight, veil herself in a red blanket (கம்பலம் செய்யது); Puram 19 has Death flee ashamed (கூற்றுக்கண் ஓடிய) on a field where mothers weep. 'The prize cannot bear the war' and the claim of an older pattern are inferences, and the Puram line is read one way among several.

Thirikadugam 10 names living beside those who lack the habit of sharing food (பாத்துண்ணும் தன்மையிலாளர் அயலிருப்பும்) as yielding no good; Kural 322 puts sharing food first of all. The neighbour's-cost angle is a small addition, so it is closer to agrees than develops.

2823 sets seed in good soil against seed in barren soil (நன்னிலத் திட்ட வித்தின் ... புன்னிலத் திட்ட வித்திற்), while Naladiyar 38 gives only the banyan seed in worthy hands (தக்கார்கைப் பட்டக்கால்). The epic does add the poor-soil case and the quatrain the scale of the good-soil case, and the note and teaches are accurate on both.

2386 has the astrologer set out the days for the king and 1062 has the astrologers fix a day for another bride. These are separate weddings, so nothing in 1062 is developed, and the 108 elephants and seven-day festival are not in the packet text.

Both verses use the moon's spot to excuse the poet's fault: Soolamani 5 says his fault is no fault before the good (திங்கண் மறுவுஞ் சிலர்கைதொழச் செல்லும்), Neelakesi 6 says even the moon is not spotless and he will not refuse to own a fault (யானும் ஒட்டாமை உண்டோ). The contrast of plea and confession is true to both lines, though the topos is conventional.

1418 leaves an unnamed man burning at the defeat (அனல்படு மனத்தன்) and 1419 has Ratna Greevan lift a mountain in rage; that the first man is the second is the marker's guess. It is story sequence, and the lesson about anger and grief is generic.

935 says the beaten dog fell in the net of strong karma (வல்வினையார் வலைப்பட்டது) and 1108 has women say 'see the fruit of deeds' at Civakan's arrest (வினையது விளைவு காண்மி). Neither verse names the god's rescue or Civakan's deed to the dog, so the irony in teaches comes from outside the units.

245 has the king say life would fall apart if the harassing stopped (அலைசெய்வதொழியின் வாழ்க்கை அழியும்); 252 answers that even killing in intent leads to hell (செயிர்தரு நரகின் அல்லால் செல்லிடம் இல்லை). That is a refuted claim and its answer, but the sage does not speak to 'rule needs killing' or 'costs more than it gives', which the teaches line adds.
links.text_issue: speaker of 245 tangled between sage and king

links.reason: 293 has the tormentors make the queen eat her own limbs (தன்னவயவம் ... தின்னும்) and Naladiyar 123 has the crab-eater's fingers rot when the old deed comes home. Both show retribution matching the act, but one does not extend the other, so parallel_domain fits better than develops.

1946 line 1 gives 'seven, three cubits, six fingers' for the first layer and line 4 has முழு வில் ஐஞ்ஞூற்றொடு, matching Neelakesi 92's five hundred bows (பேரளவ் ஐஞ்ஞூறுவில்) and its yojana. The two Jain texts share one table of hell body-sizes, and the Neelakesi figure helps read the Soolamani line.

1215 has the god foretell the friends coming 'like stars that lost the moon' (வெண்மதி இழந்த மீன்போல்) and 1761 has them wasting 'like a summer hill' (வேனிற் குன்றென) and only thinking what to do. The wasting fits the foretelling but the verse does not show them setting out, so 'part of the plan' is inferred.

1381 reproaches Civakan as one who walks the path of grace yet shows none to her (அருடேர் வழிநின்று ... அருளாய்); Kural 1154 is about those who trusted an assurance (தெளித்தசொல் தேறியார்). 1381 mentions no earlier assurance, so the 'gap between word and deed' is read in and the shared word is அருள்.

565 has the king say envoys are made as the voice of the machine called king (வாயாத் தூதுவர் இயற்றப்பட்டார்); 108 foretells a man bearing a letter. 565 mentions no letter, and an envoy being the sender's mouth does not make him part of the receiver's body, so teaches misdescribes the verse.

67 has Yugi move the kin to Pushpakam (கொண்டு வந்து வைத்தனன்) and resolve to answer the victors with guile (வஞ்சனை செய்வோம்); that is at most பேணிக்கொளல். Division and reconciling are not shown, and 'appoints rulers' is not in the verse, so the 'three skills' mapping is stretched.

2671 says the king is the love-god of the love-god (காமற்குங் காமனே) among women; Tirumanthiram 203 says even the learned are infatuated with bewildering women (மருள்கொண்ட மாதர் மயலுறுவார்கள்). The only common thing is women, and 'the praise states how firm the hold is' and 'just before his turning away' are not in either text.

356 has the deity conceal her land and lineage (நாடும் ... குலனும் தெய்வம் கரந்து); 1787 has Vijayai say her clan is not easy to tell and ask theirs first (நும்குலமும் நும்வரவும் நீருரைமின்). Both show concealment of identity, but that it became her 'habit' and that recognition waits on their story is an inference.

354 has Vijayai refuse the milk-nectar offered in a gold vessel (நேர்ந்து நோக்கா); 2624 says a woman who once drank boiled milk from a golden bowl now begs, because of cruel deeds. The note says she 'would give anything for' milk, which misreads 2624, and the beggar's wanting is not in the verse.

57 has Naga Kumaran subdue a maddened elephant (நாகத்தை அடக்கிக்கொண்டு) and Silappathikaram 15:42-53 has Kovalan free the Brahmin and tame one (கடக்களிறு அடக்கிய கருணை மறவ). The taming of a rogue elephant is a common feat; the 'royal suspicion' in teaches is not in verse 57.

2148 has Govindan laugh that the wretch calls Death with his own hand (காலனை ... கையினால் விளிக்கும்); 2174 has Kattiyangaran, not knowing Death has camped outside (கூற்றம் வந்து புறத்திறுத்தது), send gifts. The later verse turns the jest into fact, and the note says so on both ends.

97 shows a rutting elephant bowing at the vina's song (கேட்டு வந்தடி பணிந்தது); Tirumanthiram 977 has five elephants of the senses held by the goad of five letters (அஞ்செழுத்து அங்குசம்). Reading the real elephant as the passions is imposed on the epic, and the other side gains no outward counterpart from it.

227 says effort cannot prevail once the deity has settled the end (தெய்வம் முடிப்புழி என்செய்யும்) and Kural 619 grants the deity may deny the end but effort still pays a wage (மெய்வருத்தக் கூலி தரும்). Both concede the end can be lost, so the difference is a floor Kural adds, a qualification more than a tension.

Kalittokai 61 lines 11-12 (ஈதல் இரந்தார்க்கு ஒன்று ஆற்றாது வாழ்தலின் சாதலும் கூடுமாம்) carry Kural 230's thought in other words, so the giving ethic is applied in an akam scene. The teaches line that it 'obliges the girl to yield' is the marker's reading; the poem does not draw that conclusion.

161 praises Saccandan's spear and fame (வானம் தோய் புகழான் மலிவு எய்தினான்) and mentions no woman; Kural 1088 is a lover's complaint that his might broke before her forehead. The fall by desire is told in 9 and elsewhere, so the link depends on hindsight and the gains clauses are not in the verse.

183 likens Vijayai to Tirumakal on the lotus (திருமகள் இவள் என); 232 has Tirumakal leave the king without a word of leave (திருமகள் ஒளித்து நீங்க). The same goddess is named, but 232 does not say the loss comes through his absorption in her, and Tirumakal is a stock figure.

228 has Dattai sit dejected as Mananigai is named; 237 has Mananigai strike the ball eight thousand times (எண்ணாயிரம் அடித்தனள்), answering the earlier scores. The answer to the gloom is real, but it is story sequence in one contest and the lesson drawn is generic.

95 describes a throne carved with a fanged beast gripping an elephant calf (கவ்வி ... எயிற்ற வாளி) and its lord; 723 has the prince tear a real lion (வாளெயிற்று இடை வலித்து அடக்கையிற் பிடித்தான்). That the lord of 95 is the prince, so that he outdoes the emblem, is not in either verse.
